source_reviews.independent_solution: An electric field drives free electrons in a metal (or ions in an electrolyte) into directed motion. Their interactions with the constituent particles transfer electrical energy into internal energy and can warm the conductor. Current is not consumed, and charge carriers do not need to stop or accumulate to create heating. For the stationary purely resistive metal model, electrical work supplies the thermal energy; generated heat is not necessarily the conductor's own internal-energy increase because some energy may leave for the surroundings.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For a stationary purely resistive conductor under constant U and I during t, A=UIt and all electrical work becomes thermal energy, so Q=A=UIt. Use volts, amperes and seconds to obtain joules. This equality concerns generated heat, including heat subsequently transferred out, not necessarily the conductor's retained energy. Do not extend Q=A to an electric motor's mechanical output or an electrolytic cell's chemical conversion.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Joule-Lenz law in the model is Q=I^2Rt. Holding R and t fixed gives Q proportional to I^2, so multiplying I by k multiplies Q by k^2. Holding I and t fixed gives Q proportional to R. Holding I and R fixed gives Q proportional to t. These are controlled comparisons, not a claim that the higher-resistance element always heats more in every circuit. At fixed U and t in an ohmic purely resistive conductor, substitution I=U/R instead gives Q=U^2t/R, reversing the resistance comparison.

source_reviews.independent_solution: A secure low-resistance electrical contact reduces localized resistive heating and its associated overheating hazard; a loose or inadequately joined contact can have a large contact resistance. For the same through-current over the same duration, the junction's heat is I^2*R_contact*t, so lowering contact resistance lowers localized generated heat. This is not removal of all wire resistance or elimination of current. In a real supplied circuit changing contact resistance can also change I, so the controlled-current assumption must accompany a strict comparison. The source asks for the purpose and physical basis, not instructions to solder or dismantle a supply circuit.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Removing an energized immersion heater from water does not necessarily stop electrical heating. Heat removal becomes much less effective without surrounding water. If incoming electrical heating exceeds outgoing thermal transfer, the heater's internal energy and temperature rise and it may quickly fail. It is unnecessary and generally unjustified to assume the current grows or that the resistance falls upon removal; the decisive explanation is continued heat input with impaired cooling. The event is a fault analysis only, never an experiment to attempt.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The three wires in series carry the same current and are energized for the same time, hence Q_copper:Q_steel:Q_cupronickel=R_copper:R_steel:R_cupronickel. For equal length L and cross-sectional area S, R=rho*L/S, so the heat ranking is the resistivity ranking under the stated comparison. For the usual classroom materials one expects cupronickel to have the highest resistivity and heat most, with ordinary steel above copper. However this seed provides no resistivity table, specified alloy compositions, temperature conditions or measured resistances, so that exact named-material ordering is an additional material-property premise, not deduced from the selected definitions alone. The fully seed-supported answer is conditional: the greatest resistance/resistivity produces the most heat at the common current and time. Teacher-led low-voltage demonstration can measure or compare heating safely; actually observing and explaining its evidence is a separate capacity from selecting an algebraic relation.
